content: El Tor is the name assigned to a specific strain of the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, which is the pathogen responsible for causing cholera. This strain, also referred to as O1, has been the predominant strain during the seventh global cholera pandemic. Genetically, El Tor is distinct from the classical strain of Vibrio cholerae, although both strains belong to the O1 serogroup and share the same serotypes: Inaba, Ogawa, and Hikojima. The El Tor strain was first identified in 1905 at a quarantine camp in El-Tor, Egypt. It was later detected again during an outbreak in 1937. However, the pandemic associated with this strain did not emerge until 1961, when it began in Sulawesi, Indonesia. From there, El Tor spread across Asia, reaching Bangladesh in 1963 and India in 1964. Subsequently, it expanded into the Middle East, Africa, and Europe. By 1973, the strain had spread from North Africa into Italy. During the late 1970s, smaller outbreaks were reported in Japan and the South Pacific. The widespread nature of the El Tor pandemic can be attributed to several factors. First, the strain is relatively mild in its clinical presentation, with lower levels of disease severity compared to the classical strain. This mildness results in a significantly higher proportion of asymptomatic carriers, with asymptomatic cases outnumbering symptomatic cases by as much as 50 to 1. Additionally, El Tor has a prolonged persistence within the human body and demonstrates greater environmental survivability compared to other strains of Vibrio cholerae. The infection caused by El Tor is generally less severe and rarely fatal. Furthermore, unlike the classical strain, El Tor is capable of direct host-to-host transmission, which has likely contributed to its extensive spread during the pandemic.
